$comment: The broker's local control protocol, as a fixture both languages read. Node: src/control-server.js and bin/handoff-admin.mjs, held against this file by test/control-protocol.test.js. Python (Hermes side, later slices): the drop control client. Nothing here is secret and nothing here is a credential.

transport.exchange: one request line out, one response line back, then the server closes
transport.exchange_note: True of every op except the file claim, which is the one multi-message conversation on this socket: `begin_file_claim` answers with a metadata line, then the connection alternates length-framed binary out with `ack_frame` lines in, one per file, and finishes with a `commit_file_claim` line and its answer. See `file_claim` below. Nothing else on this socket ever writes a byte that is not part of a newline-terminated JSON line.
transport.max_response_bytes_note: The response line every conforming client must be able to buffer. Only `claim` can approach it — base64 of the broker's maxPlaintextBytes (65536 by default) is 87,384 bytes — so it is stated once here rather than derived twice. A client whose reader is smaller does not get to be silent about it: it advertises its real ceiling on `claim` and is refused before anything is consumed.
transport.min_response_bytes_note: The floor under an advertised max_response_bytes; anything smaller is refused with invalid_request. It bounds the `claim` op only, because that is the only op the ceiling applies to: every answer `claim` can give other than a payload — `unavailable` (35 bytes), `invalid_request` (39) and `response_too_large` (114 at its widest, with both counts spelled out in full) — fits inside it, so a conforming client can always read the answer it gets, refusals included. It says nothing about the other ops: a `create` response carrying a rendered notice is ~570 bytes and could grow, which is why transport.max_response_bytes, not this, is the line every client must be able to buffer. A ceiling below this floor could only produce a line the caller cannot read, which would surface as a transport fault for what is really a configuration mistake.
transport.size_convention: Every byte count here is of the whole line as written to the socket, including the terminating newline. That is the unit a reader has to budget for: asyncio's StreamReader, for one, applies its limit to the line plus its separator.

payload_kinds_note: The payload kinds this broker can mint, echoed on every `create` response as `payload_kinds`. Additive and deliberately *not* a protocol version bump: a client that never sends `payload_kind` gets exactly the text drop it always got, and a client that needs file drops reads this list and refuses before posting a link rather than discovering a text-only broker at submit time. Absence of the field means text only. A `text` drop carries one UTF-8 secret under max_plaintext_bytes in envelope v1; a `files` drop carries one HDROP2 container under the file limits in envelope v2, and its bytes are NOT retrievable through `claim` — they come out over the framed transfer described in `file_claim`.

outbound_drop.direction: The other direction, and the only one in this protocol where the caller supplies the payload: Hermes already holds a short secret and wants the *user* to receive it instead of reading it in chat (docs/OUTBOUND_SECRET_DROP_MVP.md). Everything else here is a user sending a secret in; `create_outbound_drop` is a secret going out. It is a separate record space with its own ids, capabilities, states and seams — an outbound drop is not a payload kind of a handoff and cannot be claimed, awaited or transferred by any op above.
outbound_drop.advertised_as: Published as `outbound_protocol` on every `create` response as well as on `create_outbound_drop`'s own, so a plugin learns the capability from the first call it makes rather than from the call it makes after deciding to post a secret. Absence means this broker cannot hand a secret out at all, whatever else it advertises. Revision 1 *is* the lifecycle below; a change to it raises this number rather than reinterpreting it.
outbound_drop.stored: Ciphertext only. The broker encrypts the plaintext with a fresh AES-256-GCM key before storing anything, wipes the buffer the plaintext arrived in, and then **drops the key** — it is handed back inside the URL fragment and nowhere else. This is the one place in the project where the broker does not hold the decryption key, and it is free, because nothing on the broker ever needs to read an outbound payload. What a record holds is ciphertext, an IV, and a keyed verifier of the code. Never the plaintext, never the key, never the code. The caveat that applies to `claim` in the other direction applies here too: the base64 the secret arrived as is an immutable JS string on the broker's heap until it is collected, so 'wiped' is about buffers, not about strings (SECURITY.md).

code.note: A 3-digit decimal code, generated by the broker and returned once on `create_outbound_drop` so the caller can post it *separately from the link*. It never appears in the URL, in page metadata or in any public response. It is a human-presence and anti-preview gate, not a second factor: it stops an unfurler, a scanner or an antivirus from consuming the drop, and it is not strong authentication when the link and the code travel in the same conversation. Only the claim operation may present it. What the broker stores is HMAC-SHA256 over the code under a per-record random key, compared in constant time.
code.attempts_note: Three incorrect codes destroy the payload. At three digits the attempt budget *is* the rate limit — 1000 candidates is not a search anything else can bound — and the MVP states the trade plainly: denial of delivery is preferred over allowing online brute force. A wrong code on a live drop is the one public refusal that is not the uniform body, because three attempts are worthless if a user cannot tell a mistyped code from a dead link; the third one collapses back into the uniform refusal, because by then the drop really is over. A malformed code or claim id costs no attempt: a shape mistake is the client's, not the user's.

states: available -> reserved by one claim id (correct code) -> destroyed (acknowledged)
available | reserved -> destroyed (TTL lapse, ack window lapse, shutdown)
outbound_drop.claim_id: A non-guessable reservation token, not a bearer credential and not a secret the broker keeps — but not a value that may be treated as public either, because it carries two powers for the life of the ack window: it replays the ciphertext, and it is the only thing `POST /api/reveal/ack` checks before destroying the payload. Rules for a client: draw it from a CSPRNG (16 bytes), keep it inside the page's own session, and never put it in a URL, a query string, a log line, an analytics event, a `postMessage` or durable storage outside that session. Anyone holding the link *and* the id can destroy the drop before the user reads it. The broker compares it in constant time, and a presented value of the wrong length is the uniform refusal rather than an error.
outbound_drop.one_browser: The reservation is taken synchronously, in the same step that verifies the code, so two browsers arriving together with the same correct code cannot both leave believing they won. The loser is answered with the uniform body — it may not be told that someone else is revealing the drop right now. Once reserved, a *different* claim id is refused however correct its code.
outbound_drop.same_claim_retry: A reserved drop answers the claim id that reserved it with the identical ciphertext, IV and deadline, for as long as its bounded ack window lasts. What that survives is precisely a **dropped response and a re-sent request** — the same page, holding the same claim id, asking again. It is deliberately not a second delivery: nothing is re-sealed, no deadline is extended, and no second claimant becomes possible. A retry with the wrong code is refused without a hint and without spending an attempt, because the budget bounds guessing at an *available* drop.
outbound_drop.same_claim_retry_does_not_survive_a_relo: Stated separately because it is the loss mode a reader will otherwise assume away. A page reload draws a **fresh** claim id and loses the reserved one, and from that point the user cannot get the secret: `POST /api/reveal/metadata` answers the uniform body for a reserved drop, so the gate cannot even be rendered; `POST /api/reveal/claim` with the new id answers the uniform body however correct the code; and the payload is destroyed at the end of the ack window regardless. There is no re-request path — a drop is one-shot and no control op reports its fate — so a background kill, a pull-to-refresh or an OS memory reclaim between the code and the copy costs the secret. This is the accepted consequence of one-browser reservation in U1, not a bug to work around in a client. The fix belongs to the browser slice: persist the claim id in the page session *before* the claim is sent, and let metadata answer a reserved drop to a caller that presents that drop's own claim id — which resumes the legitimate claimant without making a second one possible, since the id is 128 bits and unguessable.
outbound_drop.destruction: The payload dies at the acknowledgement or at the end of the ack window, whichever comes first, and the record is removed from both indexes — so a destroyed outbound drop and one that never existed are the same thing to every seam. The window is what makes 'destroyed after reveal' true for a browser that reveals and then vanishes; it is clamped inside the drop's own expiry, and expiry and shutdown reach a reserved drop like any other.
outbound_drop.fragment: <base>/#r.<capability>.<key> — the scheme marker, the capability and the base64url AES key, all three in the fragment, which browsers never send to a server. The key therefore appears in no request, no access log, no unfurl and no page metadata. The marker exists because one link format serves both directions and a page has to tell them apart before it fetches anything, which it cannot ask a server to do for it.

endpoints.POST /api/reveal/metadata: Non-secret status for a live, unreserved drop: `did`, `alg`, `code_length`, `attempts_remaining`, `expires_at`, `ack_window_ms` and the broker's own `now` for a countdown. `ack_window_ms` is the window this drop can actually honour — the configured window clamped to the drop's own remaining life — not the configured number, because a claim clamps its deadline the same way and a page renders its pre-claim countdown from this field. No ciphertext, no IV, no code, no verifier. It consumes nothing and may be fetched repeatedly. A reserved drop answers the uniform body here — the only party entitled to hear more is the one holding its claim id, and it hears it at the claim endpoint.
endpoints.POST /api/reveal/claim: The code gate and the reservation, and the only operation that returns ciphertext. Body: `{ code, claim_id }`, where `claim_id` is 22 base64url characters (128 bits) the *browser* draws. Answers `revealed` with `{ did, alg, iv, ct, claim_expires_at }`, `code_incorrect` with `attempts_remaining`, or the uniform body.
endpoints.POST /api/reveal/ack: The acknowledgement, and the thing that destroys the payload. Body: `{ claim_id }`, and it is honoured only for the claim id that holds the reservation — the code is not re-checked here, so the claim id alone is what authorizes destruction. One-shot: the record is gone afterwards, so a repeated ack is the uniform body, which is the truth.

public.statuses_note: Public HTTP statuses, deliberately NOT entries in this protocol's `errors`: those are the vocabulary of lines that come off the control socket, and these are bodies a browser reads. `unavailable` is the same 404 and the same body the inbound endpoints use, for the same set of reasons — unknown, malformed, expired, reserved by someone else, out of attempts, already acknowledged — and `code_incorrect` is a 403 carrying nothing but the count that remains.
public.safe_previews: All three endpoints are POST and none of them is reachable by GET or HEAD, which is a requirement rather than a convention: the landing page has to survive being previewed by Telegram, Discord, Slack, an antivirus and a link checker, and a claim a scanner could trigger would be a secret consumed by a preview. A GET or HEAD of any of them — with or without a capability — answers the uniform body and changes nothing: no reservation, no attempt, no destruction.
public.liveness_disclosure: One qualification on the one-browser rule above, stated because it is true rather than because it is desirable. `POST /api/reveal/metadata` consumes nothing, spends no attempt and is not rate-limited, and it flips from 200 to the uniform body the instant a reservation is taken — so anyone holding the link can poll it and learn *when* the correct code was entered. They cannot separate that transition from a TTL lapse or a spent attempt budget, and they cannot act on it: the drop is reserved to a claim id they do not have. It is disclosure of activity timing to an audience that already holds the link, which on this platform is everyone who can read the conversation, i.e. the accepted audience. It is accepted rather than closed because removing the distinction would cost the gate its countdown and its attempt display for no attacker-relevant gain.
public.decryption: The browser decrypts locally with the key from the fragment. AES-256-GCM, with the drop id as additional authenticated data, so ciphertext sealed for one drop cannot be opened as another's even by a holder of both keys — a page served the wrong ciphertext gets an AEAD failure rather than a plausible string. Production is HTTPS-only: plain HTTP cannot protect browser-delivered decryption code from an active network attacker, and `crypto.subtle` does not exist outside a secure context.

file_claim.advertised_as: Revision 1 *is* the conversation below, acks included — there is no earlier revision 1 with a different shape, and a change to the shape has to raise this number rather than reinterpret it. Published as `file_claim_protocol` on the `create` response; absence means this broker can mint a `files` drop but cannot transfer its bytes, which is exactly what a slice-2 broker is. A client that needs file drops checks BOTH `payload_kinds` and this field, and refuses before posting a link — discovering it after the user has already uploaded 42 MiB is a drop that can only lapse.
file_claim.why_not_claim: `claim` answers with one newline-delimited JSON line, so delivering a 42 MiB container through it would mean base64 in a ~57 MB line that both sides must hold whole. The transfer below streams instead: the broker writes views into the container it already holds, and neither side ever assembles a second copy.
conversation: 2. broker answers one metadata line: the transfer id, the lease deadline, the total byte count and one entry per file (name, size, type) in transfer order

3. broker writes the frame for file 0 and then WAITS: uint32 big-endian length, then exactly that many bytes. The length always equals the entry's `size`, and a zero-length frame is a legitimately empty file — its header is the whole frame
4. client reads that frame, hashes it, and sends one `ack_frame` line naming the transfer, the index, the size it read and the SHA-256 it computed
5. broker checks the ack against the manifest and only then writes the next frame; steps 3-4 repeat until every file has been acked
6. client sends one `commit_file_claim` line carrying the byte count it received and the SHA-256 it computed over each file's received bytes
7. broker verifies, retires the payload, answers one line, and closes
file_claim.receipt:
Why the frames are acked one at a time instead of streamed and totalled at the end.

The broker's byte counter used to be fed by socket write completions, which mean the kernel accepted the bytes and not that the peer read them. For any payload smaller than the socket send buffer — a tunable, 208 KiB on an ordinary Linux host — every frame therefore 'completed' before the receiver had read a byte, so a receiver that committed straight after the metadata line was accepted. Above that size the same receiver was refused. A rule that holds for a 42 MiB drop and silently does not hold for a 16 KiB one is worse than no rule: it is absent for the most common drops and looks present in a test.

An ack is the fix because it cannot be produced by the kernel. The broker sends one frame and stops; the receiver has to read it and hash it to answer; the broker checks that answer against the manifest before it writes anything else; and `commit_file_claim` is refused unless every frame was acked. Nothing about that depends on a buffer size, so a receiver that commits a step early is refused identically at 16 bytes and at 42 MiB — including for a drop of only empty files, whose frames must still be acked.

The irreducible limit, unchanged and stated plainly: a caller that already knows the plaintext can compute any ack or digest it likes without reading anything. No exchange on this socket can distinguish that caller from an honest one, because the digests are of content it holds. The socket is 0600 and the caller is already trusted with the payload, so this is not a disclosure path — but `commit → ok` is a statement about an honest receiver having received the bytes, not a proof against a dishonest one. What the acks do buy, uniformly and regardless of size, is that an *ordinary or buggy* receiver cannot retire a payload it has not read.
file_claim.lease: Exactly one transfer lease may exist per handoff, and it is bound to the connection that opened it — there is no lease token to present on a second connection, so a lease cannot be stolen or forged by a caller who learns a transfer id. The lease has a bounded deadline (`lease_expires_at`) which is never later than the handoff's own expiry, and every way it can end without a commit — disconnect, timeout, a failed commit, handoff expiry, broker shutdown — returns the handoff to `submitted` with the payload intact.
file_claim.turn_taking:
The numbered conversation above is strictly turn-taking, and the broker enforces it by *structure* rather than by timing. Each op is accepted in exactly one state of the conversation: `ack_frame` only while a frame is outstanding, and `commit_file_claim` only once every frame has been acked. Anything else — a commit pipelined behind the begin, a commit sent instead of an ack, an ack for a frame that is not the outstanding one, a second begin — is refused with `invalid_request` and the lease is released.

Enforcing it structurally is what makes it size-independent. An earlier revision inferred the same rule from *when* data arrived relative to the frames going out, which is a fact about the socket send buffer rather than about the receiver, and is also a race for large frames: a receiver can legitimately answer before the broker's own write completion fires. Neither problem exists when the rule is 'the outstanding frame must be acked first'.

Inbound data is bounded rather than paused. The broker keeps reading — pausing would move an early line into the kernel and then deliver it looking timely, removing the evidence rather than the behaviour — and caps what it retains at one request line's worth, dropping the connection past that.
file_claim.digests_are_not_echoed: The metadata line deliberately does NOT carry each file's SHA-256, even though the broker knows it: a digest the receiver was handed is a digest the receiver can return without reading a byte. The receiver computes each digest over the bytes it actually received — once per frame in its `ack_frame`, and again over the whole set in its commit — and the broker compares them against the manifest before it advances. One limit remains, and it is irreducible rather than a gap to close: a digest only binds a caller that does not already know the content (see `receipt`). Within that limit the broker's `ok` on commit is the strongest verdict available to a receiver, and stronger than its own self-check: a receiver that writes files to a spool must publish them only after it, never before.
file_claim.commit_is_the_only_retirement: Nothing about a file transfer consumes the payload until the broker has accepted a commit. A transfer that fails at any point costs a refusal and leaves the handoff `submitted`, one-shot and claimable by the next `begin_file_claim` until its TTL lapses. `begin_file_claim` may be repeated after a failure, but not without limit: each granted lease costs a full digest pass over the container, so a handoff grants a bounded number of them (see `begin_file_claim.errors`) and refuses further attempts rather than destroying the payload.
file_claim.lease_lost_mid_conversation: The connection is closed without a final line. Writing a refusal instead is not possible in general — binary frames may be in flight, and a JSON line inserted between them would corrupt the stream — so one behaviour is used for every phase rather than two that differ by timing. What a receiver may conclude depends on whether it had already written its commit. Before the commit: nothing was consumed, and the transfer may be retried — that is `transfer_failed`. After the commit: the broker may have accepted it, retired the payload and lost only the answer, so the outcome is **indeterminate** and neither `transfer_failed` nor success may be reported. See `client_verdicts`.
file_claim.client_verdicts_note:
Verdicts a *receiver* produces about its own transfer. They are not in `errors` because the broker never sends them: `errors` is the vocabulary of lines that come off the socket, and a receiver has to be able to say something the socket did not.

`transfer_indeterminate` means the commit was written and no answer was read — because the connection closed, or because the receiver's own deadline elapsed after it had written the commit. `commit_file_claim` is one-shot, non-idempotent and not requeryable, so this outcome is genuinely unknown rather than failed: the payload may have been retired, or may still be waiting.

Safe caller semantics, and there is only one safe set: **do not publish** anything received (the verification verdict never arrived), **do not retry** the transfer (a retry answered `unavailable` is indistinguishable from a drop that was already claimed, so a retry cannot resolve the ambiguity and can only compound it), and **do not record the drop as spent** (it may not be). Keep whatever was staged out of reach, surface the drop id for an operator, and let the TTL settle it. A receiver that maps this onto `transfer_failed` is asserting the payload survived, which it does not know; one that maps it onto success is asserting it was verified, which it also does not know.

version_notes.lossless_claim: Version 2 added `max_response_bytes` on `claim`, the `response_too_large` error and `protocol_version` on the `create` response. Only a version 2 broker refuses an oversized claim *before* consuming it; a version 1 broker accepts the field, ignores it, and destroys the payload as it answers. A client therefore reads `protocol_version` rather than assuming the capability from its own age — the field is absent on version 1, and absence means 1.
version_notes.file_claim: The framed transfer (`begin_file_claim` / `commit_file_claim`, the `transfer_failed` error, `file_claim_protocol` on `create`) is additive and deliberately *not* a version 3. Nothing a version 2 client sends or reads changed: it never names the new ops, never receives `transfer_failed` — that error is reachable only from them — and ignores one more field on `create` exactly as it already ignores `payload_kinds`. Versioning it would have forced every text-only client to widen its accepted-version check for a capability it will never use, and the capability is already advertised as a field a client can test for.
version_notes.compatibility: Additive. A version 1 client sends no new field and reads no new field, and behaves against a version 2 broker exactly as it did against a version 1 one.

error_notes.invalid_request: A caller mistake: unknown op, missing or ill-typed field, oversized line, unsupported notice_platform, unusable max_response_bytes, an op sent in a phase the connection is not in — including a `commit_file_claim` while a frame is still outstanding, which is how an early commit is refused whatever the payload's size. Never a statement about a handoff.
error_notes.unavailable: One body for missing, malformed, expired, consumed and lapsed. A content invariant, not a timing one: `await` blocks only for a live pending handoff and therefore leaks liveness to its local caller by construction.
error_notes.transfer_failed:
The two file-claim ops only. When the broker sends it, it means exactly one thing and a client may rely on it: **nothing was consumed**. The payload is untouched, still `submitted`, still one-shot, and still claimable by the next `begin_file_claim` until the TTL lapses. It is deliberately distinguishable from `unavailable`, which a client is entitled to read as "this drop is over": a transfer that hit a busy lease, a lapsed lease or a digest mismatch must not be recorded as a spent drop, because that would manufacture the loss the refusal just prevented. It carries a `reason` for local diagnosis — `transfer_in_progress`, `lease_expired`, `lease_not_yours`, `transfer_id_mismatch`, `incomplete_transfer`, `size_mismatch`, `digest_mismatch`, `handoff_expiring`, `attempt_budget_spent` — which is a statement about the transfer and never about a payload, a filename or a caller's identity. `ack_frame` adds `frame_ack_mismatch` and `frame_ack_out_of_order`, and `commit_file_claim` adds `frames_not_acked`. Reachable only through the 0600 socket, by a caller already trusted with the plaintext.

The guarantee is scoped to refusals the broker actually spoke. A receiver that never read an answer knows nothing about what the broker did, and must not borrow this error to say it does: if it had already written a commit, the outcome is `transfer_indeterminate` (see `file_claim.client_verdicts`). A receiver may still use `transfer_failed` for a failure of its own that provably preceded the commit — an abandoned stream, a truncated read — because in those cases no commit existed to be accepted.
error_notes.response_too_large: `claim` only, and only when the caller advertised a max_response_bytes the answer would not fit in. Nothing is consumed: the payload is untouched, still one-shot, and still claimable by a reader that can hold it until the TTL lapses. Carries required_bytes and max_response_bytes so an operator can act on the mismatch. It is deliberately distinguishable from `unavailable` — it is a statement about the caller's own reader, not about the handoff — and it does tell that caller a payload of that size is waiting. Acceptable for the same reason `await`'s timing leak is: `claim` is reachable only through the 0600 socket, by a caller already trusted with the plaintext.

create.summary: Mint one handoff and return its one-time URL.

ttl_seconds.note: Defaults to the broker's ttlSeconds (1800); must be > 0 and <= maxTtlSeconds (3600).

notice_platform.note: Opt-in. When present, the response also carries notice, notice_received and notice_expired. An unlisted value is refused with invalid_request and mints nothing.

payload_kind.note: Defaults to `text`, which is the drop this protocol has always minted. An unlisted value is refused with invalid_request and mints nothing. A `files` drop additionally reserves its advertised maximum total against the broker's process-wide live-file budget at create time; when that budget is full the creation is refused with the uniform `unavailable` and nothing is minted.

max_files.note: Only meaningful with payload_kind `files`, and refused with invalid_request on a text drop rather than ignored. A positive integer that may only *narrow* the operator's HANDOFF_MAX_FILES; a larger value is clamped down to it. Narrowing the count does not reduce the reservation, because one file may still be the whole per-drop byte total.

response.protocol_version: number: the protocol this broker speaks; absent means 1
response.payload_kinds: array of the payload kinds this broker can mint; absent means ["text"]
response.file_claim_protocol: number: the framed file-transfer revision this broker speaks (see file_claim); absent means it cannot transfer file bytes at all, whatever payload_kinds says
response.outbound_protocol: number: the outbound-drop revision this broker speaks (see outbound_drop); absent means it cannot hand a secret out at all. Advertised on this response as well as on create_outbound_drop's, so the capability is known before anything is posted
response.payload_kind: string: the kind this handoff was minted as, `text` or `files`
response.handoff_id: 22 base64url characters; non-secret and safe to log
response.url: <base>/#<capability> — the capability rides in the fragment and appears nowhere else
response.max_plaintext_bytes: number; text drops only — the secret cap says nothing about a file drop and is not quoted at one
response.max_files: number; files drops only — the count this drop will accept, after any narrowing
response.max_file_bytes: number; files drops only — the per-file cap, with max_total_bytes remaining authoritative
response.max_total_bytes: number; files drops only — the cap this drop reserved against the live-file budget
response.notice: only when notice_platform was given: the waiting message, rendered for that platform
response.notice_received: only when notice_platform was given: the content the waiting message is edited into on submit; identical on every platform
response.notice_expired: only when notice_platform was given: the content it is edited into on lapse; identical on every platform

create_outbound_drop.summary: Mint one outbound drop: encrypt a short secret the caller already holds, store the ciphertext, and return the link, the code and nothing else. The only op on this socket that carries plaintext *in* — see `outbound_drop` for the lifecycle it starts.

plaintext_b64.note: The secret, as canonical base64 — strictly decoded, so a value with a wrong alphabet, wrong padding or trailing junk is refused rather than silently reinterpreted. At most HANDOFF_MAX_OUTBOUND_PLAINTEXT_BYTES (2048) bytes, which is what keeps a whole outbound request inside transport.max_request_bytes. This is a short private value, not a file: outbound file sharing is explicitly out of scope. It is decoded, encrypted and wiped within the call, and never echoed in the response.

ttl_seconds.note: Defaults to HANDOFF_OUTBOUND_TTL_SECONDS (1800 for this deployment), which is a separate dial from the inbound HANDOFF_TTL_SECONDS even where the two agree. Bounded by the outbound ceiling HANDOFF_MAX_OUTBOUND_TTL_SECONDS (3600, itself narrow-only against HANDOFF_MAX_TTL_SECONDS) — NOT by the inbound maximum, so an operator can shorten outbound exposure without shortening the window an inbound drop gets. Floor: the effective lifetime must be at least 1000 ms. A shorter one is refused rather than minted, because a drop that lapses before the message carrying its link renders is answered with the uniform body, which is byte-identical to the one a secret somebody else took produces — the user could not tell the two apart, and no op reports which happened. Type-checked, not coerced: a boolean or a numeric string is invalid_request, never a silently accepted value.

response.protocol_version: number: the protocol this broker speaks; absent means 1
response.outbound_protocol: number: the outbound revision this broker speaks (see outbound_drop)
response.drop_id: 22 base64url characters; non-secret and safe to log. A separate id space from handoff_id — no op above accepts one
response.url: <base>/#r.<capability>.<key> — the capability AND the decryption key ride in the fragment and appear nowhere else
response.code: the 3-digit code, returned exactly once. Post it separately from the url; it must never appear in the link, in page metadata, in a log or in any public response
response.max_code_attempts: number: 3 — incorrect codes before the payload is destroyed
response.ack_window_ms: number: how long a reserved drop waits for its claimant's acknowledgement before destroying the payload anyway
response.ttl_seconds: number: the lifetime actually granted, which is the value asked for or the configured default — never a clamp, because an out-of-range request is refused rather than adjusted

errors.invalid_request: missing, ill-typed, non-canonical, empty or oversized plaintext_b64; a ttl_seconds that is not a number, is under the 1-second floor, or is above the outbound ceiling. Nothing is minted, and the decoded plaintext buffer is wiped on every one of these paths as well as on success
errors.unavailable: the uniform refusal, for the same reasons every other op can give it

await.summary: Block on the submission event. Answers with a status and an id, never with the payload.

wait_ms.note: Defaults to 0. The broker never waits past the handoff's own expiry.

claim.summary: Consume the payload exactly once. The only op that returns plaintext. Text drops only: a `files` drop answers `unavailable` here, untouched and still one-shot, because a container is not something to base64 into one newline-delimited line. Its bytes come out over the framed transfer of slice 3.

wait_ms.note: Defaults to 0. When > 0, blocks on the submission event first, so nothing polls.

max_response_bytes.note: The caller's own reader ceiling for one response line in bytes, newline included (see transport.size_convention); must be an integer between transport.min_response_bytes and whatever the caller can really hold. When present the broker sizes the whole response *before* consuming anything and answers response_too_large rather than retire a payload the caller could not have received. Absent means the caller reads an unbounded line and wants no such check — which is what bin/handoff-admin.mjs does, and is why it stays the recovery path for a payload some other reader is too small for. Only honoured by protocol_version 2 and above: a version 1 broker ignores it silently, which is what the version field on `create` is for.

response.plaintext_b64: base64 of the payload bytes — transport encoding for the JSON line, not a protection measure

begin_file_claim.summary: Take the one transfer lease on a submitted `files` drop and stream its bytes. Phase 1 of 2: it hands over bytes and consumes nothing. Files drops only — a `text` drop answers `unavailable` here, exactly as a `files` drop does at `claim`.

lease_ms.note: A positive integer that may only *narrow* the broker's own lease (HANDOFF_FILE_CLAIM_LEASE_MS, 60000 by default); a larger value is clamped down to it. A receiver that knows it writes to a slow disk cannot buy more time here — that is an operator's decision, because the lease is what bounds how long one drop can hold the live-file budget hostage. Ill-typed values are refused with invalid_request rather than ignored. The result is additionally clamped to the handoff's own remaining time, so `lease_expires_at` is never a deadline the broker cannot honour; when too little of the TTL is left to be worth streaming for, the begin is refused with `transfer_failed` / `handoff_expiring` *before* any bytes move, rather than after a full transfer the commit could not have settled.

response.transfer_id: 22 base64url characters, fresh per lease. Not a credential: the lease is bound to this connection, so the id only lets a commit name which transfer it is committing.
response.lease_expires_at: epoch milliseconds; the frames and the commit must both land before it
response.total_bytes: number: the sum of every entry's size, and exactly how many payload bytes the frames carry
response.files: array in transfer order of { name, size, type }: the display name the manifest carried (already canonical — never a path and never to be joined onto one), its exact byte length, and the untrusted MIME hint, which may be empty. No digest — see file_claim.digests_are_not_echoed
response.then: the frame for file 0, on this connection, immediately after this line. The broker then waits for its `ack_frame` before writing file 1

errors.unavailable: unknown, expired, still pending, already claimed, or a text drop
errors.transfer_failed: reason `transfer_in_progress`: another connection holds the lease, including one that took it during this request's own manifest pass. reason `handoff_expiring`: too little of the handoff's TTL is left for a transfer to be committable. reason `attempt_budget_spent`: this handoff has already granted its bounded number of leases without a commit; the payload is still there and still lapses on its TTL, but no further manifest pass will be spent on it. Nothing was consumed in any of the three
errors.invalid_request: missing or ill-typed handoff_id or lease_ms, or a connection that already holds a lease

ack_frame.summary: Acknowledge one frame the receiver has read and hashed, so the broker will send the next. It consumes nothing and it is the step that makes receipt size-independent (see file_claim.receipt). Accepted only on the connection holding the lease, and only for the frame that is currently outstanding.

transfer_id.note: The transfer id this connection's begin_file_claim answered with.

index.note: The position in the manifest of the frame being acked. Must be exactly the outstanding one: acks are strictly in order, and an index that is not the expected one is a refusal rather than something to reorder.

size.note: How many bytes that frame delivered. Must equal the manifest entry's size.

sha256.note: 64 lowercase hex characters, computed over the bytes that frame actually delivered. Compared against the container's own manifest, which the broker has and the receiver was never given.

response.index: number: the frame that was acked
response.next_index: number: the frame the broker has just written and is now waiting on, or null when that was the last one — at which point the only op left is commit_file_claim

errors.transfer_failed: reason `frame_ack_mismatch` (the size or the digest disagrees with the manifest) or `frame_ack_out_of_order` (an index other than the outstanding one). Nothing was consumed; the lease is released and a fresh begin_file_claim can try again
errors.unavailable: the handoff was destroyed under the transfer, or was already claimed
errors.invalid_request: missing or ill-typed fields, a connection that holds no lease, or an ack sent when no frame is outstanding

commit_file_claim.summary: Acknowledge a fully received and verified transfer, and retire the payload. The last step, and the only thing in the protocol that consumes a `files` drop. Accepted only on the connection that opened the lease, and only once every frame has been acked.

handoff_id.note: Must be the handoff this connection's lease is on.

transfer_id.note: Must be the transfer id the matching begin_file_claim answered with.

received_bytes.note: Total payload bytes the client actually received across all frames, length prefixes excluded. Must equal total_bytes.

digests.note: One 64-character lowercase-hex SHA-256 per file, in transfer order, each computed over the bytes that file's frame actually delivered. The broker compares them against the container's own manifest; a mismatch is a refusal and not a retirement.

response.files: number: how many files were transferred
response.bytes: number: how many payload bytes were transferred

errors.transfer_failed: reason `lease_expired`, `lease_not_yours`, `transfer_id_mismatch`, `frames_not_acked`, `incomplete_transfer`, `size_mismatch` or `digest_mismatch`. Nothing was consumed; the handoff is back to `submitted` and a fresh begin_file_claim can try again
errors.unavailable: the handoff was destroyed during the transfer, or was already claimed — there is nothing left to commit. Rare on the wire and deliberately so: a destroy drops the lease holder's connection, and the lease deadline is clamped inside the handoff's own TTL, so a receiver normally meets a closed connection rather than this line. It remains reachable in the narrow race where a commit is processed after the handoff lapsed but before the release reached the socket, and it is the answer an in-process caller gets
errors.invalid_request: missing or ill-typed fields, a connection that holds no lease, or a commit sent while a frame is still outstanding — the early-commit case, refused identically at every payload size (see file_claim.receipt). A commit is never accepted on a connection that did not open the transfer, whatever ids it names

cli.rule: exit 0 means the payload is waiting: claim it. Any non-zero means do NOT claim.

exit_codes.1: transport failure — socket unreachable, request timed out, or the answer was malformed; the payload's fate is genuinely unknown
exit_codes.2: usage — a caller mistake, never a statement about the handoff
exit_codes.3: the broker answered unavailable: expired, consumed, or the wait lapsed
